resources.string: Overview of device status and key hardware parameters.
The lowest frequency the CPU can scale down to during idle periods to save battery.
The highest frequency the CPU can scale up to under heavy load for maximum performance.
Algorithm that controls how the CPU frequency scales up or down based on system load.
Management of frequency and scaling for the Graphics Processing Unit.
The lowest clock speed the GPU will use in 2D or low-load scenarios.
The maximum clock speed for high-performance 3D gaming and UI rendering.
Logic responsible for GPU power management and frequency stepping.
Prevents overheating by throttling performance or shutting down components when temperature limits are reached.
Temperature at which the kernel starts reducing CPU/GPU frequencies to cool down.
Critical temperature at which specific CPU cores are disabled to prevent hardware damage.
Virtual memory allows the system to compensate for physical RAM shortages by storing data in compressed form.
Allocates a portion of physical RAM to be used as a compressed swap device, effectively increasing available memory.
Determines the trade-off between compression ratio and CPU overhead. LZ4 is typically the fastest.
Controls how aggressively the kernel swaps data from physical RAM to Z-RAM. Higher values increase multitasking capability but can slow down the UI under heavy load.
Governs the tendency of the kernel to reclaim memory used for caching directory and inode objects. Lower values keep more cache in RAM, potentially speeding up file access.
Maximum percentage of memory for dirty pages. High values allow more data to be cached before writing to disk, improving burst performance.
Percentage of memory at which background disk writes begin. Lowering this can prevent sudden I/O spikes.
Forces the kernel to keep a specific amount of RAM free. Can prevent LMK lag by having memory ready for new apps.
Delays disk write-backs while the screen is on to improve UI responsiveness and save battery.
The I/O scheduler decides the order in which read and write requests are sent to the storage device.
Predicts future read requests by loading more data than requested into RAM. Larger values can improve sequential read speeds.
Algorithm used to optimize disk access. Examples: CFQ (fairness), Deadline (latency), NOOP (for SSDs).
Disabling software Cyclic Redundancy Check can improve write performance by skipping data verification overhead.
Manage configuration profiles to quickly switch between performance, balanced, and battery-saving modes.
Configure app behavior and global application settings.
Automatically re-applies all saved kernel settings after the device has finished starting up.
Wait specified time after boot before applying settings. Useful if system is still initializing.
Synapse is a comprehensive kernel management tool providing advanced control over CPU, GPU, Memory, and more.
Inspired by the legendary Synapse app by AndreiLux and apb_axel.
Miscellaneous advanced kernel settings. Do not change them unless you know what you are doing.
Low-power sleep states for Qualcomm Krait CPUs. C0 is shallowest (fast wake), C3 is deepest (power collapse).
Deduplicates identical memory pages in RAM to save space. Can increase CPU usage slightly.
An enhanced version of KSM with better performance and lower CPU overhead.
Dynamically adjusts memory pressure thresholds to prevent system lag when RAM is low.
Tries to schedule system tasks on more power-efficient cores to save battery.
Controls file system synchronization. Disabling increases speed but risks data loss on crash.
Allows blocking specific drivers from keeping the device awake to improve deep sleep.
General system utilities and global kernel toggles.
Quick access to reboot into specialized system modes.
Determines how the network stack handles data flow. Different algorithms can optimize WiFi/LTE speeds.
Disabling Android logging can slightly improve performance and reduce overhead.
Hotplug drivers dynamically enable or disable CPU cores to save power during low system load.
Use only one hotplug driver at a time. Using multiple can cause system instability.
Modern scheduler that uses a power model to decide task placement for best efficiency.
Restricts specific groups of processes to a subset of CPU cores (e.g., system tasks on efficient cores).
Boost technologies temporarily increase CPU/GPU performance in response to user interaction.
Increases CPU frequency when touch input is detected to improve responsiveness.
Specifically for the GPU, increases frequency during high-load rendering tasks.
Power efficient cores designed for background tasks and low power consumption.
High performance cores for demanding applications and multitasking.
Prime core designed for maximum single-threaded performance.
Central Processing Unit frequency scaling and governor control.
